chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter V
paragraphs: At that very time, in circumstances even more significant than retreating without a battle — namely, the evacuation and burning of Moscow — Rostopchin, usually portrayed as the instigator of that event, acted in an entirely different manner from Kutuzov.
After the Battle of Borodino, the abandonment and burning of Moscow was as inevitable as the army's retreat beyond Moscow without fighting.
Every Russian could have predicted it — not through reasoning, but through the instinct planted in each of us and in our forebears.

The same thing that happened in Moscow had happened in every town and village on Russian soil from Smolensk onward, without any involvement from Count Rostopchin and his broadsheets. The people awaited the enemy calmly, without rioting or tearing anyone apart, but faced their fate with the inner strength to know what needed to be done at the most difficult moment. And as soon as the enemy drew near, the wealthy departed, abandoning their property, while the poor remained and burned and destroyed what was left.

The awareness that this would happen — that it would always happen — was and is present in the heart of every Russian. This awareness, this premonition that Moscow would be taken, existed in Moscow society in 1812. Those who had left the city already in July and early August showed they expected it. Those who departed, taking what they could and abandoning their homes and half their possessions, did so from a latent patriotism that expresses itself not through speeches or through giving up one's children to save the fatherland and similar unnatural gestures, but quietly, simply, organically — and therefore in the way that always produces the most powerful results.

"It is disgraceful to run from danger; only cowards are fleeing Moscow," they were told. In his broadsheets Rostopchin shamed them for leaving, insisting it was a disgrace. They were ashamed to be called cowards, ashamed to go — but they left anyway, knowing it had to be done. Why did they go? One can hardly suppose Rostopchin's horror stories about what Napoleon had done in conquered countries frightened them. The first to leave were the rich and educated, who knew perfectly well that Vienna and Berlin had remained intact, and that during Napoleon's occupation the residents had spent their time pleasantly in the company of charming Frenchmen, whom Russian women in particular found so appealing.

They left because for Russians there could be no question of whether things would go well or badly under French rule in Moscow. Being subject to French rule was out of the question — it would be the worst possible outcome. They left even before the Battle of Borodino, and even faster after it, despite Rostopchin's calls to defend Moscow, his announcement that he'd take the wonder-working icon of the Iberian Mother of God into battle, and his plans for hot-air balloons to destroy the French, and all the other nonsense he published in his broadsheets. They knew it was the army's job to fight, and if the army couldn't succeed, it made no sense to send young ladies and household servants to the Three Hills to fight Napoleon — they needed to leave, however sorry they were to abandon their property. They left without dwelling on the tremendous significance of a great city being handed over to destruction — for a great city of wooden buildings, once abandoned by its inhabitants, was certain to burn. Each left on his own account, and yet only because of their leaving was the momentous event accomplished that will always remain the greatest glory of the Russian people. The lady who, fearing she'd be stopped by Rostopchin's orders, had already moved to her Saratov estate in June with her household, with a vague sense that she was not Bonaparte's servant, was truly carrying out the great work that saved Russia. But Count Rostopchin — who now taunted those leaving, now had government offices evacuated; now distributed useless weapons to drunken mobs, now organized icon processions, now forbade Father Augustin to remove icons or holy relics; now seized all private carts in Moscow and used one hundred thirty-six of them to transport Leppich's balloon; now hinted he would burn Moscow and described setting fire to his own house; now published a proclamation solemnly scolding the French for destroying his orphanage; now claimed credit for suggesting Moscow be burned and now denied it; now ordered people to catch all spies and bring them to him, now reproached them for doing so; now expelled all French residents from Moscow, now let Madame Aubert-Chalme (the center of the entire French colony in Moscow) remain, while having the venerable old postmaster Klyucharev arrested and exiled for no particular offense; now assembled the people at the Three Hills to fight the French, and now, to be rid of them, handed over a man to be killed and himself slipped away by the back gate; now declared he would not survive Moscow's fall, now wrote French verses in albums about his role in the affair — this man did not understand the meaning of what was happening. He merely wanted to do something dramatic himself, to perform some patriotically heroic feat; and like a child he played games with the momentous, unavoidable event — the abandonment and burning of Moscow — and with his feeble hand tried now to speed, now to slow the enormous popular tide that carried him along.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter VI
paragraphs: Helene, having returned with the court from Vilna to Petersburg, found herself in a difficult position.

In Petersburg she had enjoyed the special protection of a grandee who held one of the highest posts in the Empire. In Vilna she had formed an intimate relationship with a young foreign prince. When she returned to Petersburg, both the magnate and the prince were there, and both claimed their rights. Helene was faced with a new problem — how to maintain her intimacy with both without offending either.

What would have seemed difficult or even impossible to another woman caused Countess Bezukhova not the slightest embarrassment, fully justifying her reputation as a very clever woman. Had she tried concealment or cunning to extricate herself from the awkward position, she would have undermined her case by admitting guilt. But Helene, like a truly great man who can do whatever he pleases, at once assumed her position to be perfectly correct — as she sincerely believed — and that everyone else was to blame.

The first time the young foreigner dared to reproach her, she lifted her beautiful head and, half turning to him, said firmly: "That's so typical of a man — selfish and cruel! I expected nothing better. A woman sacrifices herself for you, she suffers, and this is her reward! What right have you, monseigneur, to demand an account of my attachments and friendships? He is a man who has been more than a father to me!" The prince tried to say something, but Helene cut him off.

"Well, yes," she said, "perhaps he does have feelings for me beyond those of a father. But that is no reason for me to shut my door on him. I am not a man, to repay kindness with ingratitude! Know, monseigneur, that for everything concerning my intimate feelings, I answer only to God and to my conscience," she concluded, placing her hand on her beautiful, fully exposed bosom and gazing heavenward.
"But for heaven's sake, listen to me!"
"Marry me, and I will be your slave!"
"But that's impossible."
"You won't lower yourself to marry me, you..." said Helene, beginning to cry.

The prince tried to console her, but Helene, as if completely distraught, said through her tears that nothing prevented her from marrying, that there were precedents (there were very few at the time, but she mentioned Napoleon and some other eminent figures), that she had never been her husband's wife in the true sense, and that she had been sacrificed.
"But the law, religion..." said the prince, already yielding.
"The law, religion — what were they invented for if they can't sort this out?" said Helene.
The prince was surprised that so simple an idea hadn't occurred to him, and he consulted the holy brethren of the Society of Jesus, with whom he was on intimate terms.

A few days later, at one of those enchanting parties Helene gave at her country house on the Stone Island, the charming Monsieur de Jobert — a man no longer young, with snow-white hair and brilliant black eyes, a Jesuit in lay clothing — was introduced to her. In the garden, by the light of the illuminations and to the sound of music, he spoke to her at length about the love of God, of Christ, of the Sacred Heart, and of the consolations offered by the one true Catholic faith in this world and the next. Helene was moved, and more than once tears rose to her eyes and to Monsieur de Jobert's, and their voices trembled. A dance, for which her partner came to claim her, ended her discourse with her future spiritual director, but Monsieur de Jobert came to see Helene again the next evening when she was alone, and after that he visited often.
* A lay member of the Society of Jesus.

One day he took the countess to a Roman Catholic church, where she knelt before the altar to which she was led. The enchanting, middle-aged Frenchman laid his hands on her head and, as she herself later described it, she felt something like a fresh breeze waft into her soul. It was explained to her that this was grace.

After that, a long-robed abbe was brought to her. She confessed to him, and he absolved her of her sins. The next day she received a box containing the Sacred Host, left at her house for her to partake of. A few days later Helene learned with pleasure that she had been admitted to the true Catholic Church, and that soon the Pope himself would hear of her and would send her a certain document.

Everything done around her and to her at this time — the attention devoted to her by so many clever men, expressed in such pleasant, refined ways — and the state of dove-like purity she was now in (she wore only white dresses and white ribbons throughout) gave her pleasure. But this pleasure never for a moment distracted her from her goal. And as always happens in contests of cunning — that the stupid person outwits the clever ones — Helene, having understood that the real purpose of all these words and efforts was to convert her to Catholicism in order to extract money for Jesuit institutions (she had received hints of this), insisted before parting with any money that the various steps necessary to free her from her husband should be taken. In her view, the purpose of any religion was simply to maintain certain proprieties while satisfying human desires. And with this aim, in one of her conversations with her confessor, she demanded an answer to the question: to what extent was she bound by her marriage?

They were sitting in the twilight by a window in the drawing room. The scent of flowers drifted in through the window. Helene wore a white dress, transparent at the shoulders and bosom. The abbe — a well-fed man with a plump, clean-shaven chin, a pleasant firm mouth, and white hands meekly folded on his knees — sat close to Helene. With a subtle smile on his lips and a peaceful look of delight at her beauty, he occasionally glanced at her face as he explained his views on the matter. Helene, with an uneasy smile, looked at his curly hair and his plump, clean-shaven, dark-stubbled cheeks, expecting at every moment the conversation to take a new turn. But the abbe, though clearly enjoying his companion's beauty, was absorbed in his mastery of the argument.

The Father Confessor's argument ran as follows: "Ignorant of what you were undertaking, you made a vow of marital fidelity to a man who, for his part, by entering marriage without faith in its religious significance, committed an act of sacrilege. That marriage therefore lacked the dual meaning it should have had. Yet despite this, your vow was binding. You broke it. In doing so, did you commit a venial or a mortal sin? A venial sin, because you acted without evil intent. If you now married again for the purpose of bearing children, your sin could be forgiven. But the question is again twofold: first..."

But suddenly Helene, who was getting bored, said with one of her bewitching smiles: "But I think that since I have embraced the true religion, I cannot be bound by obligations imposed by a false one."

The spiritual director was astonished at having the case presented with the simplicity of Columbus's egg. He was delighted at his pupil's rapid progress but could not abandon the edifice of argument he had so laboriously constructed.
"Let us understand one another, Countess," he said with a smile, and began refuting his spiritual daughter's arguments.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter VII
paragraphs: Helene understood that the question was quite simple from the Church's point of view, and that her spiritual directors were creating difficulties only because they feared how the secular authorities would react.

So she decided to prepare public opinion. She provoked the jealousy of the elderly magnate and told him what she had told the other suitor — that the only way for him to have a claim on her was to marry her. The elderly magnate was at first just as startled by the suggestion of marrying a woman whose husband was still alive as the younger man had been, but Helene's unshakable conviction that it was as simple and natural as marrying a single woman had its effect on him too. Had Helene herself shown the slightest sign of hesitation, shame, or secrecy, her cause would certainly have been lost; but not only did she show no such signs — on the contrary, with good-natured openness she told her close friends (which meant all of Petersburg) that both the prince and the magnate had proposed, and that she loved both and was afraid of hurting either.

A rumor immediately spread through Petersburg — not that Helene wanted to divorce her husband (had such a report spread, many would have opposed so illegal an intention), but simply that the unfortunate and fascinating Helene was torn over which of the two men to marry. The question was no longer whether this was permissible, but only which was the better match and how the court would view it. There were, admittedly, some rigid individuals who could not rise to such heights and who saw the whole scheme as a desecration of the sacrament of marriage, but there weren't many, and they kept quiet. The majority were interested in Helene's good fortune and in the question of which match would be more advantageous. Whether it was right or wrong to remarry while one's husband was living, they did not discuss — that question had obviously been settled by people "wiser than you or me," as they said, and to doubt that decision was to risk exposing one's own stupidity and inability to function in society.

Only Marya Dmitrievna Akhrosimova, who had come to Petersburg that summer to visit one of her sons, allowed herself to express an opinion contrary to the general one. Meeting Helene at a ball, she stopped her in the middle of the room and, amid general silence, said in her gruff voice: "So wives of living men have started marrying again! Maybe you think you've invented something new? You've been beaten to it, my dear! It was thought of long ago. It's done in all the brothels." And with those words, Marya Dmitrievna rolled up her wide sleeves with her usual threatening gesture, glanced sternly around, and marched across the room.

Though people feared Marya Dmitrievna, she was regarded in Petersburg as a buffoon, and of what she'd said they noticed and repeated in whispers only the one crude word she'd used, assuming the entire sting of her remark lay in it.
Prince Vasily, who lately often forgot what he'd said and repeated the same thing a hundred times, remarked to his daughter whenever he happened to see her:

"Helene, I have something to say to you," and he would lead her aside, drawing her hand downward. "I've heard about certain plans concerning... you know. Well, my dear child, you know how your father's heart rejoices to know that you... You have suffered so much. But, my dear child, consult only your own heart. That is all I have to say." And concealing his invariable emotion, he would press his cheek to his daughter's and move away.

Bilibin, who had not lost his reputation as an exceedingly clever man, and who was one of the disinterested male friends that a brilliant woman like Helene always has — friends who can never become lovers — once gave her his view of the matter at a small, private gathering.

"Listen, Bilibin," said Helene (she always called such friends by their last names), touching his coat sleeve with her white, ring-laden fingers. "Tell me, as you would a sister, what I should do. Which of the two?"
Bilibin wrinkled the skin over his eyebrows and thought, smiling.

"You're not catching me off guard, you know," he said. "As a true friend, I've thought and thought about your situation. You see, if you marry the prince" — he meant the younger man, and he crooked one finger — "you lose forever the chance of marrying the other, and you'll displease the court besides. (You know there's some sort of connection.) But if you marry the old count, you'll make his last days happy, and as a widow of the Grand... the prince would no longer be making a poor match by marrying you." And Bilibin smoothed out his forehead.

"That's what a true friend sounds like!" said Helene, beaming, and she touched Bilibin's sleeve again. "But I love them both, you know, and I don't want to hurt either. I would give my life for the happiness of both."
Bilibin shrugged, as if to say that not even he could help with that.
"A masterly woman! That's what's called having it all figured out. She'd like to marry all three at once," he thought.
* A masterly woman.
"But tell me, how will your husband view the matter?" Bilibin asked — his reputation was so well established that he didn't fear asking so blunt a question. "Will he agree?"
"Oh, he loves me so!" said Helene, who for some reason imagined that Pierre too loved her. "He'll do anything for me."
Bilibin pursed his lips in preparation for something witty.
"Even divorce you?" he said.
Helene laughed.

Among those who dared to question the legitimacy of the proposed marriage was Helene's mother, Princess Kuragina. She was constantly tormented by jealousy of her daughter, and now that the jealousy concerned a subject close to her own heart, she couldn't accept the idea. She consulted a Russian priest about the possibility of divorce and remarriage during a husband's lifetime, and the priest told her it was impossible, and to her delight showed her a Gospel passage that (as he saw it) plainly forbids remarriage while the husband lives.
Armed with these arguments, which seemed to her unanswerable, she went to her daughter's early one morning to catch her alone.
Having listened to her mother's objections, Helene smiled blandly and ironically.
"But it says clearly: 'Whosoever shall marry her that is divorced...'" said the old princess.

"Oh, Mama, don't talk nonsense. You don't understand anything. In my position I have obligations," Helene said, switching from Russian — in which she always felt her case didn't sound quite right — to French, which suited it better.
* "Oh, Mama, don't talk nonsense. You don't understand anything. In my position I have obligations."
"But, my dear..."
"Oh, Mama, how can you not understand that the Holy Father, who has the right to grant dispensations..."
Just then the companion who lived with Helene came in to announce that His Highness was in the ballroom and wished to see her.
"No, tell him I don't wish to see him. I am furious with him for not keeping his word to me."
* "No, tell him I don't wish to see him. I am furious with him for not keeping his word to me."
"Countess, there is mercy for every sin," said a fair-haired young man with a long face and nose as he entered the room.
* "Countess, there is mercy for every sin."
The old princess rose respectfully and curtsied. The young man who had entered took no notice of her. The princess nodded to her daughter and sidled out of the room.

"Yes, she is right," the old princess thought, all her convictions dissolving at the sight of His Highness. "She is right — but how is it that we, in our irrecoverable youth, didn't know it? Yet it is so simple," she mused as she got into her carriage.

By the beginning of August, Helene's plans were clearly defined, and she wrote a letter to her husband — who, she imagined, loved her very much — informing him of her intention to marry N.N. and of her conversion to the one true faith, and asking him to complete the formalities necessary for a divorce, which would be explained to him by the letter's bearer.
And so I pray God to have you, my friend, in His holy and powerful keeping — Your friend Helene.
This letter was delivered to Pierre's house while he was on the field of Borodino.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter VIII
paragraphs: Toward the end of the Battle of Borodino, Pierre — having run down from Raevsky's battery a second time — made his way through a gully to Knyazkovo with a crowd of soldiers, reached the dressing station, and seeing blood and hearing cries and groans, hurried on, still caught up in the stream of soldiers.

The one thing he now wanted with his whole soul was to get away quickly from the terrible experiences of that day and return to ordinary life — to sleep peacefully in a room, in his own bed. He felt that only under normal conditions would he be able to make sense of himself and everything he had seen and felt. But such normal conditions were nowhere to be found.

Though shells and bullets no longer whistled over the road he was traveling, on all sides there was the same thing as on the battlefield — the same suffering, exhausted, and sometimes strangely indifferent faces, the same blood, the same soldiers' overcoats, the same sounds of firing that, though distant now, still inspired terror — and in addition the foul air and the dust.
After walking a couple of miles along the Mozhaysk road, Pierre sat down by the roadside.

Dusk had fallen and the roar of guns died away. Pierre lay propped on his elbow for a long time, watching the shadows pass him in the darkness. He kept imagining a cannonball flying toward him with a terrifying whistle — then he would shudder and sit up. He had no idea how long he'd been there. In the middle of the night, three soldiers who had gathered firewood settled near him and began lighting a fire.

The soldiers, casting sideways glances at Pierre, got the fire going and set an iron pot on it, into which they broke some dried bread and added a little fat. The pleasant smell of greasy food mixed with the scent of smoke. Pierre sat up and sighed. The three soldiers were eating and talking among themselves, paying him no attention.

"And who might you be?" one of them suddenly asked Pierre, clearly meaning what Pierre himself had been thinking — namely: "If you want to eat, we'll give you some food, only let us know whether you're an honest man."

"I... I'm..." said Pierre, feeling it necessary to minimize his social standing so as to be closer to the soldiers and better understood by them. "Technically I'm a militia officer, but my men aren't here. I came to the battle and got separated from them."
"Well, well!" said one of the soldiers.
Another shook his head.
"Would you like a little mash?" the first soldier asked, handing Pierre a wooden spoon after licking it clean.

Pierre sat down by the fire and began eating the mash — as they called the food in the pot — and thought it was the most delicious thing he had ever tasted. As he bent greedily over it, scooping up large spoonfuls one after another, his face was lit by the firelight and the soldiers watched him in silence.
"Where do you need to go? Tell us!" said one of them.
"To Mozhaysk."
"You're a gentleman, aren't you?"
"Yes."
"And what's your name?"
"Peter Kirilych."
"Well then, Peter Kirilych, come along with us — we'll get you there."
In the total darkness the soldiers walked with Pierre to Mozhaysk.

By the time they neared Mozhaysk and began climbing the steep hill into town, the roosters were already crowing. Pierre walked on with the soldiers, completely forgetting that his inn was at the bottom of the hill and that he'd already passed it. He wouldn't have remembered this at all, so deep was his state of abstraction, had he not stumbled halfway up the hill upon his groom, who had been looking for him in town and was heading back to the inn. The groom recognized Pierre in the darkness by his white hat.
"Your excellency!" he said. "We were starting to despair! How is it you're on foot? And where are you going?"
"Oh, yes!" said Pierre.
The soldiers stopped.
"So you've found your people?" said one of them. "Well, goodbye, Peter Kirilych — isn't it?"
"Goodbye, Peter Kirilych!" Pierre heard the other voices repeat.
"Goodbye!" he said, and turned with his groom toward the inn.
"I ought to give them something!" he thought, reaching into his pocket. "No, better not," said another, inner voice.
There was no room to be had at the inn — they were all occupied. Pierre went out into the yard and, covering himself from head to toe, lay down in his carriage.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter IX
paragraphs: Pierre had barely laid his head on the pillow before he felt himself falling asleep, but suddenly — with almost the vividness of reality — he heard the boom, boom, boom of firing, the thud of projectiles, groans and cries, and smelled blood and powder, and a feeling of horror and dread of death seized him. He opened his eyes in fright and lifted his head from under his cloak. Everything in the yard was peaceful. Only someone's orderly splashed through the mud at the gate, chatting with the innkeeper. Above Pierre's head, some pigeons — disturbed by his movement — fluttered under the dark roof of the shed. The whole courtyard was filled with a strong, peaceful smell of stables, which Pierre found delightful at that moment. He could see the clear, starry sky between the dark roofs of two sheds.

"Thank God — no more of that!" he thought, pulling the cloak back over his head. "Oh, what a terrible thing fear is, and how shamefully I gave in to it! But they... they were steady and calm to the very end..." he thought.

They, in Pierre's mind, were the soldiers — those at the battery, those who had given him food, those who had prayed before the icon. They — those strange men he hadn't known before — stood out sharply and clearly from everyone else.

"To be a soldier, just a common soldier!" Pierre thought as he fell asleep. "To merge completely into that communal life, to be filled with whatever makes them who they are. But how do you shed all the superfluous, devilish burden of the outer man? There was a time I could have done it. I could have run away from my father, as I wanted to. Or I might have been sent into the army after the duel with Dolokhov." And the memory of the dinner at the English Club, when he had challenged Dolokhov, flashed through his mind, and then he remembered his benefactor at Torzhok. And now he pictured a solemn Masonic meeting at the English Club, and someone dear and familiar sat at the end of the table. "Yes, that's him! My benefactor. But he died!" thought Pierre. "Yes, he died, and I didn't know he was alive. How sorry I am that he died, and how glad I am that he's alive again!" On one side of the table sat Anatole, Dolokhov, Nesvitsky, Denisov, and others like them (in his dream this category was as clearly defined as the category he called they), and he heard those people — Anatole and Dolokhov — shouting and singing loudly; yet through their noise, the voice of his benefactor could be heard speaking continuously, and the sound of his words was as weighty and unbroken as the booming on the battlefield, but pleasant and comforting. Pierre couldn't make out what his benefactor was saying, but knew (the categories of thought were perfectly distinct in the dream) that he was speaking of goodness and the possibility of being what they were. And they, with their simple, kind, firm faces, surrounded his benefactor on all sides. But though they were kindly, they didn't look at Pierre and didn't know him. Wanting to speak and draw their attention, he started to rise, but at that moment his legs grew cold and bare.

He felt embarrassed, and with one arm covered his legs from which his cloak had in fact slipped. For a moment, as he adjusted it, Pierre opened his eyes and saw the same shed roofs, posts, and yard, but now everything was tinged with blue, sparkling with frost or dew.

"It's dawn," Pierre thought. "But that's not what I want. I want to hear and understand my benefactor's words." He pulled the cloak over himself again, but now neither the lodge nor his benefactor was there. Only thoughts remained — thoughts clearly expressed in words, thoughts that someone was saying or that he himself was forming.

Afterward, when he recalled those thoughts, Pierre was convinced they had been spoken by someone outside himself, though the impressions of that day had prompted them. He had never, it seemed to him, been able to think and express his thoughts so clearly when awake.

"To endure war is the most difficult submission of human freedom to the law of God," the voice had said. "Simplicity is submission to the will of God; you cannot escape Him. And they are simple. They don't talk — they act. The spoken word is silver, but the unspoken word is golden. Man can master nothing while he fears death, but he who does not fear it possesses everything. If there were no suffering, man would not know his limits — would not know himself. The hardest thing" — Pierre went on thinking, or hearing, in his dream — "is to unite in your soul the meaning of everything. To unite everything?" he asked himself. "No, not unite. You can't unite thoughts. But to harness all these thoughts together — that is what we need! Yes, harness them — harness them!" he repeated to himself with inner ecstasy, feeling that these words alone expressed what he wanted to say and solved the question that tormented him.
"Yes, one must harness — it is time to harness."
"Time to harness, time to harness, your excellency! Your excellency!" a voice kept repeating. "We must harness — it is time to harness..."

It was the voice of the groom, trying to wake him. The sun shone straight into Pierre's face. He glanced at the dirty inn yard where soldiers were watering their thin horses at the pump while carts passed out through the gate. Pierre turned away with distaste and, closing his eyes, quickly fell back onto the carriage seat. "No, I don't want that — I don't want to see and understand that. I want to understand what was being revealed to me in my dream. One more second and I would have grasped it all! But what should I do? Harness — but how can I harness everything?" And Pierre felt with horror that the meaning of everything he had seen and thought in the dream was crumbling away.
The groom, the coachman, and the innkeeper told Pierre that an officer had come with news that the French were already near Mozhaysk and that the Russian forces were leaving the town.
Pierre got up and, telling them to harness the horses and overtake him, set off on foot through the town.

The troops were moving out, leaving about ten thousand wounded behind. Wounded men were visible in the yards, at the windows of houses, and the streets were packed with them. In the streets, around the carts that were to carry some of the wounded away, shouts, curses, and blows could be heard. Pierre offered his carriage, which had caught up with him, to a wounded general he knew, and drove with him to Moscow. On the way, Pierre learned of the deaths of his brother-in-law Anatole and of Prince Andrew.
